title: Time Is Money
tagline: time as a resource to spend, save and lose
why: In English we spend, save, waste and borrow time as if it were cash. Advanced speakers use this money vocabulary without noticing, and choosing the precise verb makes you sound fluent and exact.
know: buy time, on borrowed time, pressed for time
understand: a cultural view, not a universal one
able: Talk about schedules, deadlines and priorities using money metaphors precisely.
Choose between near-synonyms like kill time and waste time.
Discuss a song, poem or story that treats time as something to save, lose or fight.
mistakes: I passed two hours in the airport to kill the time.
I killed time at the airport for two hours. Kill time has no article, and the idiom replaces passed two hours.
I'm pressed for time today. It is passive: the time pressure is on you.
It's worth of your while to visit.
It's worth your while to visit. Worth takes no of.
We need to recover the lost time.
We need to make up for lost time. This is the fixed, natural form.
I lost my time with that course.
I wasted my time on that course. Lose time is about delays; waste time is about pointless use.
bigidea: English treats time like money: we have a limited amount, we can spend it well or waste it, save it, invest it, borrow it, or run out of it. A meeting can cost us an afternoon; a shortcut can save us an hour.
This picture grew stronger with clocks, factories and hourly wages, when time literally became something you were paid for. Benjamin Franklin's maxim time is money (1748) sums it up.
Notice the mood it creates. Time is scarce, measured and always slipping away, which is why English has so many idioms about racing the clock and so few about having plenty of time.
hidden: I spent the whole weekend painting the fence.
Don't waste your time arguing with him online.
The new highway saves me twenty minutes each way.
She invested a lot of time in that friendship.
Students need to learn to budget their time.
That wrong turn cost us an hour.
We ran out of time before the last question.
It was a profitable afternoon: we cleared the whole backlog.

expressions.meaning: do something to get more time before a decision or problem arrives
expressions.example: The extension only buys us time; it doesn't solve the funding problem.
expressions.bend: Add a person: buy yourself some time. Add amount: buy a few more weeks. Also play for time (British).
expressions.note: Often suggests a delay tactic rather than a solution. Stall is more negative; buy time can be wise or sneaky.

expressions.meaning: continuing to exist or live longer than expected, but likely to end soon
expressions.example: With falling ratings, the show has been on borrowed time for a year.
expressions.bend: Usually living / be on borrowed time. Fixed core; don't change borrowed.
expressions.note: Can be serious (illness) or light (an old car). The image is a loan that will soon be called back.

expressions.example: I'm a bit pressed for time, so can we keep this short?
expressions.bend: Add degree: a little / very / hard pressed for time. Synonym: short of time.
expressions.note: A polite way to end or shorten a conversation. Less casual than I'm swamped.

expressions.meaning: worth the time or effort it takes
expressions.example: It's worth your while to read the contract carefully before signing.
expressions.bend: Change the pronoun: worth our while. Also make it worth your while (offer a reward, sometimes a bribe).
expressions.note: 'I'll make it worth your while' can hint at an under-the-table payment, so be careful in business.

expressions.meaning: do a lot of something quickly because you couldn't do it earlier
expressions.example: After years apart, the two brothers are making up for lost time.
expressions.bend: Tense changes. Fixed core: keep lost time. Often with trying to.
expressions.note: Can be warm (relationships) or practical (catching up after a strike or a closure).

expressions.example: We killed time in the bookshop until the train arrived.
expressions.bend: No article: kill time, not kill the time. Add amount: kill an hour.
expressions.note: Kill time is neutral about waiting. Waste time is critical: it implies you should be doing something useful.

expressions.meaning: trying to finish before a deadline
expressions.example: Rescue crews are working against the clock before the storm hits.
expressions.bend: Common verbs: work / race / a race against the clock. Also beat the clock.
expressions.note: Mixes our metaphor with a race: time is both money and an opponent. Very common in news headlines.

expressions.meaning: time is valuable, so don't waste it
expressions.example: Let's skip the small talk; time is money.
expressions.bend: Fixed: don't change it. Often a reason or excuse: Hurry up, time is money!
expressions.note: Made famous by Benjamin Franklin (1748). Can sound brisk or even rude in social settings; use it humorously among friends.

culture.how: In this short letter of advice, Franklin explains that a working man who idles away part of a day has not only spent money on his leisure but also lost the wages he could have earned. His maxim time is money turns lost hours into lost income, the core of this metaphor.
culture.ask: Do you agree that free time has a price? How do you decide what an hour of your time is worth?
culture.find: Benjamin Franklin Advice to a Young Tradesman 1748

culture.how: On The Dark Side of the Moon, the song begins with a crash of clocks and describes drifting through youth assuming there is plenty of time, then suddenly realizing years have gone. Time is a resource wasted without noticing until it runs out.
culture.ask: At what age, if any, did you start to feel that time was running out?
culture.find: Pink Floyd Time Dark Side of the Moon

culture.how: A love song from the album You Don't Mess Around with Jim (a number one hit in the US after Croce's death in 1973). The singer wishes he could store time like savings, keep days in a bottle and spend them later with the one he loves.
culture.ask: If you could save time in a bottle, which days would you keep, and who would you spend them with?
culture.find: Jim Croce Time in a Bottle

culture.how: The White Rabbit is always checking his watch and fretting that he is late. At the tea party, the Hatter treats Time as a person, says he quarrelled with him, and since then it is always six o'clock. Carroll is playing with idioms like killing time and wasting time.
culture.ask: Are you more like the White Rabbit, always late and worried, or the Hatter, stuck at tea time forever?
culture.find: Alice in Wonderland Mad Tea Party Hatter Time

culture.how: Published after Marvell's death, the poem argues that slow courtship would be fine if there were unlimited time, but time is racing up behind the lovers like a chariot, so they must act now. Time is a resource that is running out.
culture.ask: Is 'life is short, so act now' a good argument, or a pressure tactic? When have you heard it used?
culture.find: Andrew Marvell To His Coy Mistress

items.why: Investing time expects a future return.
Saving time means using less of it for the same result.
Budgeting means planning carefully how to use it.
Wasting time means using it for nothing useful.

pick.q: Everyone knows the old arena is ___; the city will tear it down within two years.

pick.q: After two years of lockdowns, my parents are ___ and travelling everywhere.
pick.why: Doing a lot because they couldn't before: making up for lost time.

pick.q: Our flight was delayed, so we ___ playing cards in the lounge.
pick.why: Passing time while waiting is killing time.

pick.q: The engineers worked ___ to fix the bridge before the long weekend.
pick.why: Racing a deadline: against the clock.

pick.q: My father-in-law hates long phone calls. His motto is ___.

spot.q: We were waiting for the ferry, so we killed the time in a café.
I'm pressing for time, so I'll keep this brief.
spot.why: The idiom is passive: I'm pressed for time.

spot.q: It isn't worth of your while to drive across town for that sale.
spot.why: Worth takes a direct object, with no of.

spot.q: The government's plan is only a way to purchase time until the election.
spot.why: The idiom is fixed as buy time; purchase sounds odd and overly formal.

spot.q: Since their reunion, the sisters have been making up the lost time.
spot.why: The fixed form is make up for lost time, with for and no the.

type.q: The old printer is living on ___ time; it jams every day.
type.why: On borrowed time = lasting longer than expected, but not for long.

type.q: The negotiators are racing against the ___ to avoid a strike.
type.why: Against the clock = trying to beat a deadline.

type.q: If you ___ your time well, you can finish the thesis by April.
type.why: Budget your time = plan how to use it, like money.

type.q: That detour ___ us almost two hours.
type.why: Cost us two hours = made us lose two hours, like money.

type.q: Don't ___ your time on people who never reply.
type.why: Waste time = use it on something pointless.

type.q: I've ___ a lot of time in learning Mandarin, and it's finally paying off.
type.why: Invest time = spend it expecting a future return.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about a political crisis? ___
opts: The minister bought himself a few more weeks.
The minister bought the time for himself a few weeks.
The minister made a buying of time.
bend.why: Buy can take yourself and a period of time: buy yourself a few more weeks.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural at a busy office? ___
opts: I'm pressed of time this week.
I'm hard pressed for time this week.
I'm pressing for time this week.
bend.why: Hard can intensify pressed for time. The idiom keeps for and the passive form.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural when offering a reward? ___
opts: Help us move and we'll make your while worth it.
Help us move and it will worth your while.
Help us move and we'll make it worth your while.
bend.why: Make it worth your while = offer a reward. Keep the order worth + your while.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural at an airport? ___
opts: We had three hours to kill before boarding.
We had three hours of killing before boarding.
We had three killed hours before boarding.
bend.why: X hours to kill is a common, natural variation of kill time.

pick.q: With three days left before the vote, ___ for a compromise.

pick.q: It's a long drive, but the scenery makes it ___.
pick.why: The scenery makes the time worthwhile.

pick.q: The firefighters were working ___ as the wind changed direction.
pick.why: Racing a deadline or danger: against the clock.

pick.q: We ___ the last hour of the trip listening to podcasts.

spot.q: Our team passed too much time on the first question and never finished.
spot.why: We spend (too much) time on a task. Pass time means fill time while waiting, not use it on a task.

spot.q: The striker is living in borrowed time at this club.
spot.why: The preposition is fixed: on borrowed time.

spot.q: The new software economizes us an hour every morning.
spot.why: Save takes a person + time: it saves us an hour. Economize doesn't work this way.

spot.q: The crew worked contra the clock to finish the stage.
spot.why: The idiom is against the clock.

bank.why: A review that delays a decision buys time.

bank.q: My grandmother only got a smartphone at 85, and now she texts all day as if to ___.

bank.q: I got to the dentist early and ___ reading old magazines.

bank.q: Students sat the exam ___, with only ninety minutes for six essays.
bank.why: Working under a tight time limit is working against the clock.

bank.q: She charges by the minute, because for her, ___.

bank.q: Online banking ___ me hours every month.
bank.why: Save someone time = make things quicker.

bank.q: The renovation ___ us three weekends and a lot of patience.

bank.q: Time is ___ out for a deal on the new hospital.

bank.q: Retirees often say they refuse to lose time on bad films.
